source: Hampton (1996) Emergent attributes in combined concepts (review of Hampton 1987)
finding: Early attribute-inheritance experiments show that emergent attributes in concept conjunctions are rare, even though conjunctions are not simply compositional.
numbers: Hampton 1987 (Pets+Birds etc.): strict scoring found 3 emergent attributes out of 174. Lenient scoring found 11. Five conjunctions had none. Of 37 attributes unimportant for both constituents, about 8% were important for both forms of the conjunction.
limits: Review of older studies; small attribute sets; the 1987 results are re-reported here, not re-run.
agent_relevance: Emergence is the rare, valuable part of a blend. An agent should not assume a merge produces new structure; it should check that a claimed emergent property is absent from both inputs.

source: Hampton (1996) Emergent attributes in combined concepts (Hampton 1989 'A which are not B' study)
finding: A stricter test for emergence (rated 0% true of A alone, but true of 'A which are not B') leaves almost nothing.
numbers: Six category pairs: 51 attributes had median 0% for A. 24 stayed at 0% for 'A which are not B'; 11 deviated only slightly (0-5%, noise); only 6 had 10% or more. Examples were category stretching (a tent as a dwelling).
limits: Median ratings; most true emergents came from retrieving familiar instances, not from creating novel solutions.
agent_relevance: Most apparent emergence is retrieval of a known instance. Flag 'emergent' claims that a lookup in the model's memory would explain.

source: Hampton (1996) Emergent attributes in combined concepts (Hastie, Schroeder and Weber 1990 results)
finding: Social-stereotype conjunctions produce many more emergent traits than object categories.
numbers: Hastie et al. 1990: conjunction ratings fell at least one scale step outside the range of the two constituents on 23% of trait judgments for congruent pairs and 33% for incongruent pairs (15 bipolar dimensions).
limits: Reported second-hand; emergence defined by rating position, not by independent coding of novelty.
agent_relevance: Emergence rises when the inputs conflict and the reader must explain the clash. Conflicting inputs are a useful trigger for the blend operator.

source: Hampton (1996) Emergent attributes in combined concepts (Hampton, Dillane and Oren point-of-view study)
finding: Which attributes a conjunction inherits depends on the point of view; about a third of attributes false of both inputs appeared in the conjunction.
numbers: 210 attributes over 4 pairs: only 2 true of both categories. Own-view positive attributes: 65, only 11 (17%) inherited by the conjunction. 'Other' category: 80 attributes, 69% inherited by the conjunction. 63 attributes false of both constituents, 22 (35%) true of the conjunction.
limits: Several groups of raters each; some 'emergent' items were trivial (confused, inconsistent). Gender-consistency effects were complex and larger for male than female points of view.
agent_relevance: Blend content depends on the stance taken. Prompt the agent to blend from more than one stance and compare.

source: Hampton (1996) Emergent attributes in combined concepts (Kunda, Miller and Claire 1990)
finding: Given an incongruent combination (Harvard-educated carpenter), people invent explanatory stories, which creates new attributes.
numbers: Qualitative method in the original; no effect size reported in this chapter.
limits: Qualitative; the chapter gives no N here. Original paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Explanation-seeking is a driver of emergence. An agent can ask why these two would co-occur as a blend step.

source: Song et al. (2025) Is a Peeled Apple Still Red? Evaluating LLMs ability for conceptual combination with property type
finding: CCPT benchmark: LLMs, even o1, find it harder to produce emergent properties than canceled ones, and harder still to write a noun phrase with a given emergent property.
numbers: 12,315 annotated (noun phrase, property, type) instances. Models tested: Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen2.5-72B, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, o1-mini, o1. Noun phrase completion, emergence score E: gold 59.9, human 38.0, GPT-4o spread activation with both oracles 31.7.
quote: LLMs struggle more with generating emergent properties than with canceled ones.
limits: Numbers from Table 3 (LLM-as-judge); the table layout was hard to read in text, so only clearly labelled rows are quoted. Judged by GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Generating a concept that has a required emergent property is the hard direction. Verify by checking the property against each input separately.

source: Song et al. (2025) Is a Peeled Apple Still Red? Evaluating LLMs ability for conceptual combination with property type (property type prediction)
finding: GPT-4o can tell whether a combination has a property, but is poor at saying why (emergent, inherited or canceled).
numbers: 1000 instances (250 per type). Has-property decision accuracy 82.6% (95.6% when yes, 69.6% when no). Four-way type accuracy 56.4%, human 81%. Emergent type recognised 59.6% of the time.
limits: Single model (GPT-4o) in this analysis; human 81% is from a small side check (Appendix B.4).
agent_relevance: Do not let the model label its own output emergent. Use a code-checked test (absent from each input alone).

source: Song et al. (2025) Is a Peeled Apple Still Red? Evaluating LLMs ability for conceptual combination with property type (judge validity and spread activation)
finding: LLM-as-judge relevance scores track human ratings closely, and iterating a spreading-activation prompt gives small steady gains.
numbers: Judge vs human: Pearson 0.85, Spearman 0.83. Human Fleiss kappa 0.59 (moderate). Property induction emergent E rose from 45.1 (1 iteration) to 45.8 (5); canceled 60.5 to 63.3; filter ablation gave +1.2 (emergent) and +7.7 (canceled) points.
limits: Gains are small (under 1 point for noun phrase completion); judge validity covers relevance only, not creativity.
agent_relevance: Spreading activation over related concepts with a filter helps a little. It links to the semantic network sibling subfield.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring combinatorial creativity in LLMs and humans (KOMBINE)
finding: Across 35 LLMs, blending is the hardest of three combinatorial creativity tasks; the bottleneck is finding a shared abstraction (generic space).
numbers: Mean valid rate: association 59.0%, analogy 53.4%, blend 43.4%. Models find a valid generic space 43.4% of the time, but given one, describe a coherent blended concept 97.1% of the time. Best blend score: gpt-5.6-sol 64.8; claude-fable-5 45.7; claude-opus-4.6 41.4.
quote: LLMs are 10-16 percentage points better at discovering associations and analogies than blends.
limits: Judged by a three-LLM panel (agrees with humans 75% of the time on unanimous items). Entities are random Wikidata pairs. Blend scores average several dimensions.
agent_relevance: Support the generic-space step with a check. Once the shared abstraction is valid, the model rarely fails to elaborate it.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring combinatorial creativity in LLMs and humans (KOMBINE) (human comparison)
finding: Online human adults did worse than LLMs on every task, and found blending hardest.
numbers: N = 75 Prolific adults (120 recruited, screened for AI use), 5 items per task. Valid rate humans vs LLM: association 22.1% vs 59.0%, analogy 32.9% vs 53.4%, blend 12.8% vs 43.4%. Overall score: humans 13.7; human blend score 7.4.
limits: Lay participants, no experts or artists. Skipped items scored zero, which lowers human scores.
agent_relevance: A model can beat lay humans on blend validity, so human parity is not the right bar. Use an expert or code-checked bar.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring combinatorial creativity in LLMs and humans (KOMBINE) (inventive homogeneity)
finding: Different LLMs invent the same blend properties; this is stronger for blends and for models from one provider.
numbers: 2,070 invented concepts, 7,868 properties. One in five concepts reuses 2 or more properties invented by another model. Blends are 14 times more likely to reuse other models' properties than analogies. Same-provider models are 2.3 times more likely to reuse. Similarity threshold 0.674 (99th percentile cosine).
limits: Threshold chosen by percentile; embedding choice checked in appendix.
agent_relevance: Blend diversity from one model family is low. Resampling one model gives correlated blends; vary the input pairing and framing, not just temperature.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring combinatorial creativity in LLMs and humans (KOMBINE) (association originality predicts blending)
finding: Models that make original distant associations also make better analogies and blends, consistent with Mednick's associative theory.
numbers: Association originality vs analogy originality r = 0.73 (p<1e-4), vs surprising analogies r = 0.63, vs original blends r = 0.42 (p=1e-2), surprising blends r = 0.50 (p=2e-3), valid blends r = 0.48 (p=3e-3). Task score correlations: association-analogy 0.71, analogy-blend 0.70, blend-association 0.54.
limits: Correlations over 35 models, so the unit is the model, not the item; the models are not independent (shared providers).
agent_relevance: Blend skill is partly shared with association and analogy skill; no strong case for a separate component.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring combinatorial creativity in LLMs and humans (KOMBINE) (judge reliability)
finding: Blend judging is only fair to good in reliability, so leaderboard gaps in blend quality must be read with care.
numbers: Judge reliability: blend semantic integration quality 0.67 (good), blend utility G(g) 0.67 (good), blend utility V(c) 0.48 (fair). LLM panel agrees with humans 75% on unanimous items.
limits: Reliability measured on a 60-item human subsample (30 analogy, 30 blend).
agent_relevance: Do not rely on one LLM judge to accept a blend. Use a rubric with countable parts (shared slot, emergent triple).

source: Ge and Parikh (2021) Visual Conceptual Blending with Large-scale Language and Vision Models
finding: Language models find a relevant object for a blend better than a knowledge base, and larger models do better; image generators then draw the blend.
numbers: Simile dataset precision at P@10/P@100/P@1000: BERT-Large 0.13/7.69/37.33; GPT 1.59/15.72/53.08; the largest model in the table reached 66.38 at P@1000. 20 blend descriptions (half generated, half by the authors) judged by Mechanical Turk workers.
limits: The table text was partly garbled in extraction, so some rows are not matched to model names. Small set of 20 prompts. 2021 models.
agent_relevance: Language-model association is a good source for the select-shared-property step. Scale helps.

source: Wang, Petridis, Kwon, Ma and Chilton (2023) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with large language models
finding: GPT-3 plus a knowledge base proposes connecting concepts for pop-culture blends; users found twice as many blend ideas.
numbers: Annotation: connecting concept accuracy 56.0%, 55.3%, 58.7% for the three methods; at least one of five correct 90.0%, 96.6%, 93.3%. Stage 2 scenes: 98.3% at least one related. User study N = 10: 2.03 (SD 0.84) vs 0.87 (SD 0.56) ideas per pair, Wilcoxon p<0.001. NASA-TLX mental demand 2.85 vs 5.80 (p=0.004).
limits: N = 10 students, within-subject, baseline was internet search. Ideas counted, not rated for quality.
agent_relevance: About half of single suggestions fail, but five tries give a 90%+ hit rate. Generate several connecting concepts, then filter.

source: Wang et al. (2023) PopBlends: GPT-3 attribute accuracy
finding: GPT-3 facts about the input spaces were only partly right, which limits blends built on them.
numbers: Entity attribute accuracy overall 2.86 of 5 (57%); adjectives 79%, activities 58%, catchphrases 35%. Product scenes related to the concept 89.1%, pop culture scenes 75.9% (raw 80.0% and 63.4%).
limits: GPT-3 (2021 era). Annotators were crowd workers.
agent_relevance: Input-space facts need checking before projection; invented catchphrases were the worst case.

source: Matsuhira et al. (2024) Investigating conceptual blending of a diffusion model for nonword-to-image generation
finding: Stable Diffusion shows blended concepts often, but mostly near the midpoint between the two prompt embeddings.
numbers: 1,000 noun pairs. At the 0.5 interpolation ratio, blended concept depiction 0.621 and mixed concept depiction 0.862; across all ratios 0.389 and 0.471. Concept A alone shown 0.948 at 0.5. Detected with a CLIP score threshold of 0.15.
limits: Blend detection by a CLIP threshold, not human ratings. These are depictions, not new structure with emergent logic.
agent_relevance: Equal weighting of the two inputs gives the most blends. A text agent can mirror this by balancing the contribution of each input.

source: Peng et al. (2025) Probing and inducing combinational creativity in vision-language models
finding: Best VLMs beat average humans at understanding visual blends, not experts; prompting with a blending-based three-step frame improved image creativity.
numbers: CreativeMashup: 666 artist-made mashups. Human experts winning rate 78.3%, average participants 51%. Identification: average humans 53.42% precision, 70.33% recall; Gemini-1.5-Pro 73.67% precision, 81.33% recall. Generation: 50 Prolific raters; Friedman p<=0.0001; Midjourney mean rank IEI 1.98 vs II 2.40; winning rate against experts 0.26 to 0.35.
limits: Artists still ranked best overall. Gains small for weaker models (SD3 minimal).
agent_relevance: A prompt that names the input objects, the shared attributes, and the implication works better than one that names only objects and theme. Fits the generic-space step.

source: Peng et al. (2025) IEI: concept step vs rendering step
finding: The concept step mostly worked; the rendering step lost a quarter of the good concepts. Fusion blends are easier to understand than replacement blends.
numbers: GPT-4o concept-level combination worked in 90% (36 of 40) of DALLE-3 examples; 27.8% (10 of 36) then failed visually. Two human experts agreed with GPT-4o judging at 85.1% and 81.6% on 200 comparisons.
limits: Small checks; judge agreement comes from the authors own pairwise sample.
agent_relevance: Test the concept step and the rendering step apart, since the failure can sit in either.

source: Sato (2025) The Way We Prompt: conceptual blending, neural dynamics, and prompt-induced transitions in LLMs
finding: A conceptual review that reads blending theory onto prompt behaviour; no measured effect sizes.
numbers: None reported. Claims repeatable elicitation of prompt-induced transitions and hallucinations from blending distant domains.
limits: No data, no controls, no baseline; neural analogies are speculative by the author's own words. Treat as a hypothesis source, not evidence.
agent_relevance: Warning: blending distant domains can produce fluent but ungrounded output. The agent needs a grounding check on every projected claim.

source: Turner (2013) Challenges to Blending Theory
finding: A founder concedes that experimental evidence for blending is thin and that blending is not an algorithm.
numbers: No numbers. Empirical support is in-sample generalisations tested on out-of-sample data; experiments exist (McCubbins and Turner 2013) but design is hard.
quote: the mental process itself does not appear to me to be algorithmic.
limits: Author's own defence; not independent. McCubbins and Turner experiments not opened.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model run a fixed blend algorithm and call it the theory. Use the blend as a candidate generator checked by code.

source: Gibbs (2000) Making good psychology out of blending theory, as reported in search summaries of Schmid and Ritchie
finding: Critics say blending theory is hard to falsify and infers process from products; the governing principles were added in reply.
numbers: None.
limits: Seen only through search summaries, not read. Gibbs (2000), Broccias (2004) and Ritchie (2004) not opened.
agent_relevance: The theory is a vocabulary more than a tested mechanism, so rely on LLM tests rather than on the theory's claims.

source: Bambini et al. (2016) Disentangling metaphor from context: an ERP study (also summarising Coulson and Van Petten 2002)
finding: Brain-wave evidence for integration cost in metaphor is real but partly explained by context and expectation: N400 relates to contextual expectation, P600 to interpretation.
numbers: N = 13 healthy volunteers (6F; mean age 25.92, SD 3.75), two experiments (minimal context, supportive context). Cloze pretests with 15 and 16 matched participants. Earlier studies mostly report a biphasic N400-P600 pattern.
limits: Small sample; one language (Italian); metaphor, not blending in the full sense. Coulson and Van Petten original not opened.
agent_relevance: Context given before the blend changes the result; put input-space facts in the prompt first.

source: Frontiers Hum Neurosci (2015) Metaphors are physical and abstract: ERPs to metaphorically modified nouns resemble ERPs to abstract language
finding: Novel metaphor targets usually elicit larger N400 than literal ones, but the authors high-concreteness metaphor condition did not follow that monotonic pattern.
numbers: Passage cites Coulson and Van Petten 2002, 2007; Arzouan 2007; Lai 2009 for larger N400 to novel metaphor. No effect sizes extracted.
limits: Only a passage was read.
agent_relevance: Novelty raises processing cost. It supports treating novel blends as more error-prone.

source: Dreyfus, Gupta and Redish (2015) Applying conceptual blending to model coordinated use of multiple ontological metaphors
finding: Case studies in physics teaching show an expert and a novice blending energy-as-substance and energy-as-location into one mental model.
numbers: Two episodes: a physics professor lecture and one student interview; coded by predicate and gesture analysis. No counts or effect sizes.
limits: Qualitative, 2 speakers; no test against a rival account. Existence proof only.
agent_relevance: Blending two metaphors can make an abstract concept (negative energy) usable. Helps explanations; not shown to improve accuracy.

source: Lu et al. (2026) Rethinking creativity evaluation: a critical analysis of existing creativity evaluations
finding: LLM judges of creativity agree weakly with human reviewers, which limits LLM-judged blend scores.
numbers: Research ideation contribution scores: Pearson 0.159 between humans and LLM judge; the highest correlation seen was 0.234.
quote: The Pearson correlation coefficient between human reviewers' scores and LLM evaluation scores is only 0.159.
limits: Not about blending specifically; research-ideation domain.
agent_relevance: A generic LLM judge cannot grade blend quality. Count structure instead.

source: Xi et al. (2026) Evaluating creative generative AI with conceptual blending (ACL 2026 poster)
finding: A position poster proposes scoring creativity by conceptual integration, with six rubric criteria; no results.
numbers: Rubric criteria: completeness, clarity, relevance, understanding depth, coherence, execution time. No measured data.
limits: Poster, no experiment. Claim that temperature or style prompting raises only surface novelty is untested here.
agent_relevance: Candidate rubric for blend checks; each criterion needs a code or counting test before use.

source: McCaig, DiPaola and Gabora (2016) Deep convolutional networks as models of generalization and blending within visual creativity
finding: Deep Dream and style transfer are discussed as visual blend generators; the paper gives examples and no tests.
numbers: None; qualitative examples only.
limits: No human evaluation, no benchmark.
agent_relevance: Low. Blending without a structure-mapping step blends texture, not logic.
